questions.q: René Laennec invented which instrument in 1816, partly from embarrassment about putting his ear to a young woman’s chest?
questions.e: His first one was a rolled-up roll of paper.

questions.q: Which 1895 discovery by Wilhelm Röntgen won the first Nobel Prize in Physics?
questions.e: He never patented it, so it spread round the world within months.

theme: Fantastic voyage: a trip through the body

questions.q: Isaac Asimov, born around this date, was also a professor of?
questions.e: He taught at Boston University’s medical school and wrote a biochemistry textbook.

questions.q: Swallowed food leaves the stomach through which valve?
questions.e: Pylorus is Greek for gatekeeper.

questions.q: A red blood cell squeezes through capillaries narrower than itself. About how wide is it?
questions.e: Its doughnut shape lets it fold up like a taco.

questions.q: Roughly how long does a red blood cell take to do one full lap of the body at rest?
questions.e: Cardiac output at rest is about 5 litres a minute, roughly your whole blood volume.

questions.q: Which is the only artery to carry oxygen-poor blood after birth?
questions.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen level.

questions.q: Bile is stored in the gallbladder but made in the?
questions.e: The liver makes up to about a litre a day.

questions.q: About how long is the small intestine in a living adult?
questions.e: It’s longer at autopsy, when the muscle has relaxed.

questions.q: Air travels from the trachea into tiny sacs. Roughly how many alveoli do adult lungs have?
questions.e: Spread flat, their surface would cover roughly half a tennis court.

questions.q: In the kidney, blood is first filtered in a tuft of capillaries called the?
questions.e: Together the kidneys filter about 180 litres a day, and return all but a litre or two.

questions.q: Fantastic Voyage’s miniaturised crew aimed to destroy a blood clot in the?
questions.e: Asimov wrote the novelisation of the 1966 film.

theme: Through a tube: tubes in medicine

questions.q: The drinking straw was patented in 1888. A nasogastric tube passes through the nose into the?
questions.e: Checking its tip is in the stomach, not the lung, before feeding is critical.

questions.q: Which tube is named after an Italian anatomist and connects the middle ear to the throat?
questions.e: Bartolomeo Eustachi described it in the 1500s.

questions.q: The Sengstaken–Blakemore tube is used to stop bleeding from?
questions.e: Balloons press on the bleeding veins as a temporary measure.

questions.q: A Swan-Ganz catheter is floated through the heart into the?
questions.e: A small balloon on its tip lets blood flow carry it there.

questions.q: Which tube’s cuff, if over-inflated for a long time, can damage the trachea?
questions.e: Cuff pressure is kept low to protect the tracheal lining.

questions.q: A chest drain for a pneumothorax is classically inserted in the ‘triangle of safety’. Which muscle forms its front border?
questions.e: The back border is latissimus dorsi; the base is about the level of the nipple.

questions.q: A Foley catheter is held in the bladder by?
questions.e: Frederic Foley designed it in the 1930s.

questions.q: An underwater seal on a chest drain works because?
questions.a: Air can bubble out but water stops it getting back in
questions.e: It acts like a one-way valve.

questions.q: Which Australian invented the CPAP machine for sleep apnoea, using a vacuum cleaner motor?
questions.e: Sydney, 1980. The company it spawned became ResMed.

questions.q: The Minnesota tube differs from the Sengstaken–Blakemore by adding?
questions.a: A port to suck out the oesophagus above the balloon
w: A feeding port into the jejunum
questions.e: It reduces the risk of patients inhaling saliva and blood.

theme: Seeing with your fingers: Braille, eyes and touch

questions.q: World Braille Day marks the birthday of Louis Braille. How did he lose his sight?
questions.a: An accident with a tool in his father’s workshop, then infection
questions.e: He was three. The infection spread to both eyes.

questions.q: Each Braille cell is made of up to how many raised dots?
questions.e: Two columns of three.

questions.q: Which part of the body has the highest density of touch receptors?
questions.e: Lips and tongue are close behind.

questions.q: The clear front window of the eye is the?
questions.e: It does most of the eye’s focusing.

questions.q: Which part of the eye is coloured?
questions.e: Its muscles widen and narrow the pupil.

questions.q: What’s the most common cause of blindness worldwide?
questions.e: And it’s fixable with a short operation.

questions.q: The light-sensing layer at the back of the eye is the?
questions.e: It’s actually part of the brain, grown outwards in the embryo.

questions.q: Glaucoma damages which nerve?
questions.e: Often from raised pressure inside the eye.

questions.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes night blindness?
questions.e: It’s needed to make the light-sensing pigment in rods.

questions.q: Braille readers often read at about how many words a minute?
questions.e: Close to typical reading-aloud speed.

questions.q: ‘Canary in a coal mine’ comes from miners using canaries to detect?
questions.e: Birds breathe fast and show poisoning before people do.

questions.q: Which flu is carried by wild water birds?
questions.e: H5N1 is the best-known strain.

questions.q: In folklore, which bird delivers babies?
questions.e: Stork bites are also the nickname for pink birthmarks on a baby’s neck.

questions.q: Psittacosis, a pneumonia, is caught from?
questions.e: Breathing in dried droppings or feather dust.

questions.q: ‘Crow’s feet’ are?
questions.a: Wrinkles at the corners of the eyes
questions.e: Laughing earns them.

questions.q: A ‘pigeon chest’ is when the breastbone?
questions.e: Its medical name is pectus carinatum.

questions.q: Bird eggs can cause allergy in some children. Most grow out of egg allergy by?
questions.e: Many children tolerate baked egg first.

questions.q: The plague doctor’s beaked mask was stuffed with?
questions.e: They believed bad smells (miasma) spread disease.

questions.q: A ‘goose egg’ on the head is a?
questions.a: Bump from a bruise and swelling
questions.e: Scalp bleeds a lot because it has a rich blood supply.

questions.q: Which bird lays the largest egg relative to its body size?
questions.e: A kiwi egg is about 20% of the mother’s weight.

more.label: More ICU oddities on Deranged Physiology

questions.q: A cylinder of inhaled nitric oxide, used in intensive care, is mostly?
questions.e: Medical nitric oxide comes very diluted, around 800 parts per million, in nitrogen. Neat nitric oxide is toxic and reacts with oxygen.

questions.q: Heliox helps air get past a narrowed airway because helium is?
questions.e: Lighter gas flows more smoothly through tight spots. It also makes you sound like a cartoon chipmunk.

questions.q: Propofol, the anaesthetic drug, is nicknamed ‘milk of amnesia’ because it?
questions.e: It's dissolved in a soybean oil emulsion, which is why it looks like milk.

questions.q: Rising pressure inside the skull classically causes Cushing’s reflex: high blood pressure, irregular breathing and?
questions.e: The body pushes blood pressure up to keep blood reaching the brain. A slowing pulse is a late, worrying sign.

questions.q: Methylene blue, used for some poisonings and shock, can turn urine?
questions.e: Patients are warned in advance. It still surprises the night nurse.

questions.q: In deep hypothermia, the ECG can show an extra bump at the end of the QRS called the?
questions.e: Named after John Osborn, who described it in cold dogs in 1953.

questions.q: The ‘Lazarus phenomenon’ is?
questions.a: The heart restarting on its own after CPR has stopped
questions.e: It's rare, and one reason doctors wait and watch for several minutes before confirming death.

questions.q: On 100% oxygen, healthy lungs can push the oxygen level in arterial blood above about?
questions.e: On room air it's about 80 to 100 mmHg. More oxygen in, much more in the blood, up to a point.

questions.q: Decompression sickness (the bends) is treated in a hyperbaric chamber because high pressure?
questions.e: Higher pressure shrinks the bubbles and pushes nitrogen back into solution, then it's breathed off slowly.

questions.q: Which electrolyte, when too high, gives tall ‘peaked’ T waves on the ECG?
questions.e: High potassium can stop the heart, so it's one of the few blood results that gets a phone call at 3 am.

questions.q: Astronauts on long missions lose bone density at roughly what rate?
questions.e: Weight-bearing matters: bones need load to stay strong.

questions.q: Why do astronauts’ faces look puffy in orbit?
questions.e: Without gravity, fluid no longer pools in the legs: ‘puffy face, bird legs’.

questions.q: Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome mainly affects?
questions.e: Swelling at the back of the eye can blur sight for months.

questions.q: Which inner-ear organs sense gravity and get confused in space?
questions.e: Hence space motion sickness in the first few days.

questions.q: Astronauts grow taller in space by about?
questions.e: The discs between vertebrae expand. They shrink back on Earth.

questions.q: The first person to perform a self-operation in Antarctica, removing his own appendix in 1961, was?
questions.e: A Soviet doctor, using a mirror and local anaesthetic.

questions.q: What’s the main radiation risk outside Earth’s magnetic field?
questions.a: Galactic cosmic rays and solar storms
questions.e: A Mars mission would roughly double the lifetime radiation limit of current astronauts.

questions.q: Which Galilean moon of Jupiter is thought to have a liquid ocean under its ice?
questions.e: Galileo first saw the four big moons around this date in 1610.

questions.q: In microgravity, the heart?
questions.a: Shrinks a little and becomes rounder
questions.e: It doesn’t have to pump blood uphill.

questions.q: Astronauts on the ISS exercise about how long a day?
questions.e: Treadmill with a harness, cycling and resistance machines.

theme: Motor neurone disease and the nervous system

questions.q: Stephen Hawking, born on this date in 1942, lived with motor neurone disease for about?
questions.e: Most people with MND live 2 to 5 years from diagnosis. His was unusually slow.

questions.q: Motor neurone disease (ALS) affects?
questions.a: Both upper and lower motor neurones
questions.e: That’s why stiffness and wasting appear together.

questions.q: Which senses are usually spared in MND?
questions.e: Eye-tracking can let people communicate late in the illness.

questions.q: Fasciculations are?
questions.e: Common and harmless on their own; worrying with weakness and wasting.

questions.q: Riluzole for MND works roughly by?
questions.e: It extends survival modestly, by a few months.

questions.q: Which gene expansion is the commonest genetic cause of MND and frontotemporal dementia?
questions.e: SOD1 was found first, in 1993.

questions.q: Lou Gehrig, whose name is given to ALS in the US, played?
questions.e: He retired in 1939.

questions.q: The ‘split hand’ in MND means wasting of?
questions.a: Thumb-side muscles more than little-finger side
w: Little-finger side more than thumb side
questions.e: A clue doctors look for.

questions.q: Hawking spoke through a computer controlled late in life by?
questions.e: An infrared sensor on his glasses detected cheek twitches.

questions.q: Edaravone, used for MND in some countries, is?
questions.e: Evidence for benefit is limited.

questions.q: The iPhone was unveiled on this date in 2007. ‘Texting thumb’ is usually?
questions.e: Inflamed tendons at the base of the thumb.

questions.q: ‘Cubital tunnel syndrome’ from holding a phone to your ear with a bent elbow squeezes the?
questions.e: Tingling in the ring and little fingers.

questions.q: Blue light from screens at night mainly affects sleep by suppressing?
questions.e: Light, of any colour, tells the brain it’s daytime.

questions.q: ‘Text neck’ refers to?
questions.a: Neck and upper back strain from looking down
questions.e: Tilting the head forward multiplies the load on the neck.

questions.q: Phones carry bacteria. Compared with a toilet seat, studies often find phones carry?
questions.e: Toilet seats get cleaned more often.

questions.q: Which eye problem from screen use causes dry, tired eyes?
questions.e: We blink less when staring at screens.

questions.q: The ‘20-20-20 rule’ suggests every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for?
questions.e: It relaxes the focusing muscles.

questions.q: ‘Phantom vibration syndrome’ is?
questions.a: Feeling a phone buzz that didn’t
w: Hearing a ring in your ear
questions.e: Most heavy phone users report it.

questions.q: Which phone feature helps paramedics even when your phone is locked?
questions.e: Paramedics can see allergies, medicines and contacts.

questions.q: Hearing damage from earbuds depends on volume and?
questions.e: The 60/60 rule: under 60% volume, under 60 minutes at a time.

questions.q: The UN General Assembly first met on this date in 1946. The WHO’s constitution came into force in?
questions.e: 7 April 1948, now World Health Day.

questions.q: Which disease is the only human disease eradicated so far?
questions.e: Declared eradicated in 1980.

questions.q: Polio remains endemic in which two countries?
questions.e: Wild poliovirus cases have fallen by over 99% since 1988.

questions.q: Guinea worm disease is close to eradication, largely through?
questions.a: Filtering drinking water and health education
questions.e: The Carter Center led the campaign.

questions.q: Which infection kills the most people worldwide each year?
questions.e: Over a million deaths a year.

questions.q: The ‘Alma-Ata Declaration’ of 1978 championed?
questions.e: Health for all through community-based care.

questions.q: Which country has the highest life expectancy at birth, in most recent estimates?
questions.a: Japan, Monaco or Hong Kong (they trade the top spot)
questions.e: Australia sits in the top ten.

questions.q: ‘Universal health coverage’ means?
questions.a: Everyone gets needed care without financial hardship
questions.e: One of the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

questions.q: Oral rehydration solution is a mix of water, salt and?
questions.e: The glucose helps the gut absorb the salt and water. It has saved millions of children.

questions.q: Which mosquito-borne disease has a vaccine (RTS,S) recommended by WHO since 2021?
questions.e: A second, R21, followed in 2023.

questions.q: On this date in 1922, Leonard Thompson became the first person given insulin. He was?
questions.e: In Toronto. A purer second dose worked.

questions.q: Which organ makes insulin?
questions.e: In the islets of Langerhans.

questions.q: Insulin lowers blood sugar by?
questions.e: Muscle, fat and liver all respond.

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes happens because?
questions.a: The immune system destroys insulin-making cells
questions.e: It’s not caused by lifestyle.

questions.q: A ‘hypo’ is when blood sugar is too?
questions.e: Sweaty, shaky and confused: give fast sugar.

questions.q: Which two scientists shared the 1923 Nobel Prize for insulin?
questions.e: Banting shared his money with Best, who was left out.

questions.q: Insulin is usually injected, not swallowed, because?
questions.a: Stomach acid and enzymes digest it
questions.e: It’s a protein.

questions.q: Which number test shows average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months?
questions.e: It measures sugar stuck to haemoglobin.

questions.q: Early insulin was extracted from?
questions.e: Since the 1980s, it’s been made by genetically engineered microbes.

questions.q: World Diabetes Day is held on Frederick Banting’s birthday, which is?
questions.e: The blue circle is its symbol.

questions.q: Charles Perrault, born on this date, wrote Sleeping Beauty. Sleeping for years is a bit like which real condition?
questions.e: Rare episodes of sleeping up to 20 hours a day for weeks.

questions.q: Rapunzel’s hair could hold a prince. A single human hair can hold about?
questions.e: A full head of hair could, in theory, hold a couple of elephants.

questions.q: Snow White fell asleep after eating?
questions.e: Apple seeds do contain a little cyanide-releasing chemical, but you’d need to chew a lot.

questions.q: Pinocchio’s nose grew when he lied. A long, bulbous red nose is called?
questions.e: A complication of rosacea.

questions.q: The Princess and the Pea: feeling a pea through mattresses is a sign of?
questions.e: In real life, prolonged pressure on the same spot causes pressure sores.

questions.q: Puss in Boots is a cat. Cats can’t taste?
questions.e: They lack a working sweet-taste gene.

questions.q: Rumpelstiltskin spun straw into gold. Gold has been used in medicine to treat?
questions.e: Gold injections were common before modern drugs.

questions.q: Little Red Riding Hood’s grandmother had big eyes. Bulging eyes can be a sign of an overactive?
questions.e: Graves’ disease.

questions.q: Sleeping Beauty pricked her finger on a?
questions.e: Finger-prick tests today check blood sugar.

questions.q: Cinderella’s glass slipper: tight shoes can cause a painful bump at the big toe called a?
questions.e: Medically, hallux valgus.

questions.q: In carbon monoxide poisoning, a pulse oximeter usually reads?
questions.e: It can’t tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. A blood gas with co-oximetry can.

questions.q: Methaemoglobinaemia classically makes a pulse oximeter read about?
questions.e: Chocolate-brown blood is the bedside clue.

questions.q: Why does a patient on ECMO sometimes have bright red blood in the legs but blue fingers?
questions.a: ‘Harlequin’ or north–south syndrome from mixing of flows
w: A blood clot in one arm
questions.e: Well-oxygenated ECMO blood meets poorly oxygenated blood from the patient’s own heart.

questions.q: The ‘P’ in PEEP stands for?
questions.e: Positive end-expiratory pressure keeps small airways open.

questions.q: A tension pneumothorax on a ventilator often first shows as?
questions.a: Rising airway pressure and falling blood pressure
questions.e: Needle or finger decompression comes before the X-ray.

questions.q: Propofol infusion syndrome is a rare but deadly problem with?
questions.a: High doses for a long time
questions.e: Acidosis, heart failure and muscle breakdown.

questions.q: Which drug, given for ventricular arrhythmias, can turn skin blue-grey with long use?
questions.e: It also affects the thyroid, lungs and liver.

questions.q: The ‘lethal triad’ in major trauma is hypothermia, acidosis and?
questions.e: Each makes the others worse.

questions.q: Why can giving oxygen raise carbon dioxide in some people with COPD?
questions.a: Mostly through changes in lung blood flow and the Haldane effect
w: Oxygen turns into CO2 in the lungs
questions.e: ‘Loss of hypoxic drive’ is only a small part of the story.

questions.q: A ‘Lazarus sign’ in brain death is?
questions.a: A spinal reflex that can raise the arms
questions.e: It comes from the spinal cord, not the brain, and can distress families.

more.label: More ICU oddities on Deranged Physiology

questions.q: Albert Schweitzer, born on this date in 1875, founded a hospital in?
questions.e: He was also an organist and won the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by a parasite called?
questions.e: Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous.

questions.q: Which insect spreads sleeping sickness?
questions.e: African trypanosomiasis.

questions.q: Chagas disease is spread by?
questions.e: They bite near the lips at night, hence the name.

questions.q: Dengue is spread by which mosquito?
questions.e: Aedes bite in the daytime.

questions.q: Which drug, from cinchona bark, was the first effective malaria treatment?
questions.e: It gives tonic water its bitter taste.

questions.q: Artemisinin, from sweet wormwood, won Tu Youyou a Nobel Prize in?
questions.e: She found the method in a 1,600-year-old Chinese text.

questions.q: Leprosy mainly damages the skin and?
questions.e: Loss of feeling leads to unnoticed injuries.

questions.q: Yellow fever gets its name from?
questions.e: It damages the liver.

questions.q: Australia’s tropical north has which melioidosis-causing bacterium in its soil?
questions.e: Cases spike after heavy wet-season rain.

questions.q: Wikipedia launched on this date in 2001. Myth or fact: we only use 10% of our brains?
questions.e: Scans show activity across the whole brain.

questions.q: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis?
questions.e: A doctor cracked one hand for 60 years and found no difference.

questions.q: Hair and nails keep growing after death?
questions.e: Drying skin retracts, making them look longer.

questions.q: You lose most of your body heat through your head?
questions.e: Any uncovered part loses heat. Babies’ heads are relatively big, though.

questions.q: Sugar makes children hyperactive?
questions.e: Parents who think their child had sugar rate them as more hyperactive.

questions.q: Reading in dim light ruins your eyesight?
questions.e: It can tire your eyes, but no lasting harm.

questions.q: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker?
questions.e: The blunt tip just feels coarser.

questions.q: Swallowed gum stays in your gut for seven years?
questions.e: It passes through like other indigestible things.

questions.q: You should wait 30 minutes after eating to swim?
questions.e: No good evidence of cramps causing drowning.

questions.q: Vaccines cause autism?
questions.e: The original 1998 paper was retracted and its author struck off.

questions.q: US Prohibition was ratified on this date in 1919. Which enzyme does most of the work breaking down alcohol in the liver?
questions.e: It turns ethanol into acetaldehyde.

questions.q: The ‘Asian flush’ after drinking is due to?
questions.e: A variant of ALDH2. It also raises oesophageal cancer risk.

questions.q: Disulfiram (Antabuse) makes people sick when they drink by blocking?
questions.e: Acetaldehyde builds up.

questions.q: Wernicke’s encephalopathy in heavy drinkers is from lack of which vitamin?
questions.e: Give thiamine before glucose.

questions.q: Australia’s guideline is no more than how many standard drinks a week?
questions.e: And no more than 4 on any one day.

questions.q: A standard drink in Australia contains how much pure alcohol?
questions.e: A pint of full-strength beer is about 2.

questions.q: Alcohol makes you wee more by blocking which hormone?
questions.e: Hence the dehydrated hangover.

questions.q: Delirium tremens from alcohol withdrawal usually starts?
questions.a: 2 to 3 days after the last drink
questions.e: It can be fatal without treatment.

questions.q: Methanol poisoning damages which organ especially?
questions.e: Its breakdown product, formic acid, harms the optic nerve.

questions.q: A ‘holiday heart’ after a binge is usually which rhythm?
questions.e: Often settles once sober.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin, born on this date in 1706, is credited with inventing?
questions.e: He cut two lenses in half and joined them.

questions.q: Franklin also designed a flexible urinary catheter for?
questions.e: His brother John had bladder stones.

questions.q: Who invented the modern clinical thermometer, small enough to read in five minutes?
questions.e: Earlier ones were a foot long and took 20 minutes.

questions.q: The first successful human-to-human blood transfusion with blood typing was possible after Karl Landsteiner discovered blood groups in?
questions.e: He won a Nobel Prize in 1930.

questions.q: Willem Einthoven built the first practical ECG machine, weighing about?
questions.e: Patients put their limbs in buckets of salty water.

questions.q: The Australian-invented bionic ear (cochlear implant) was pioneered by?
questions.e: First implanted in Melbourne in 1978.

questions.q: Spray-on skin for burns was developed by?
questions.e: Used after the 2002 Bali bombings.

questions.q: Which Australian developed the HPV vaccine technology with Jian Zhou?
questions.e: Now preventing cervical cancer worldwide.

questions.q: Franklin noticed lead poisoning among?
questions.e: He linked ‘dry gripes’ to handling lead type.

questions.q: Franklin’s ‘glass armonica’ was later blamed, wrongly, for?
questions.e: People thought its eerie tones overstimulated the nerves.

questions.q: Peter Roget, born on this date, wrote the first thesaurus and was also a?
questions.e: He started his word lists to cope with depression.

questions.q: ‘-itis’ at the end of a word means?
questions.e: Tonsillitis: inflamed tonsils.

questions.q: ‘-ectomy’ means?
questions.e: Appendicectomy: removing the appendix.

questions.q: ‘Cardio’ refers to the?
questions.e: From Greek kardia.

questions.q: ‘Derma’ refers to the?
questions.e: Dermatologists are skin doctors.

questions.q: ‘Hepato’ refers to the?
questions.e: Hepatitis: liver inflammation.

questions.q: ‘Nephro’ and ‘renal’ both refer to the?
questions.e: Greek and Latin, respectively.

questions.q: ‘Brady-’ means?
questions.e: Bradycardia: slow heart rate.

questions.q: ‘Haem-’ or ‘hem-’ refers to?
questions.e: Haemorrhage: bleeding.

questions.q: ‘-scope’ means an instrument for?
questions.e: Endoscope, microscope, stethoscope.

theme: Gothic medicine: Poe and premature burial

questions.q: Edgar Allan Poe, born on this date in 1809, wrote about being buried alive. Fear of this is called?
questions.e: Some Victorian coffins had bells for the ‘dead’ to ring.

questions.q: Poe’s ‘The Tell-Tale Heart’ is about a heartbeat. A normal adult resting heart rate is?
questions.e: Athletes can sit lower.

questions.q: What’s the medical name for a death-like trance with rigid limbs?
questions.e: Victorians feared it was mistaken for death.

questions.q: Which disease killed Poe’s wife, Virginia, and was called ‘consumption’?
questions.e: It ‘consumed’ the body.

questions.q: Ravens are clever. Which part of the brain handles memory?
questions.e: Named for its seahorse shape.

questions.q: Poe’s ‘Masque of the Red Death’ features a disease that makes victims bleed from the?
questions.e: Fictional, but echoing plague and cholera fears.

questions.q: Doctors today confirm death with checks including no breathing, no heartbeat and?
questions.e: Done carefully, over several minutes.

questions.q: Stiffening of the body after death is called?
questions.e: It starts in a few hours and passes in a day or two.

questions.q: Poe died aged 40 in mysterious circumstances in which city?
questions.e: Theories range from rabies to beating.

questions.q: A ‘safety coffin’ often had a?
questions.e: ‘Saved by the bell’ is often linked to these, probably wrongly.

questions.q: Penguin Awareness Day: emperor penguins dive for over 20 minutes partly by?
questions.a: Storing oxygen in muscle myoglobin and slowing the heart
questions.e: Their heart rate can drop to a few beats a minute.

questions.q: The mammalian diving reflex is triggered mainly by?
questions.e: It slows the heart: one trick for stopping SVT.

questions.q: Adenosine for SVT is given as a fast push because it?
questions.a: Lasts only seconds in the blood
questions.e: Patients often describe a brief sense of doom.

questions.q: Why does an endotracheal tube sometimes end up in the right main bronchus?
questions.a: It’s wider and more vertical than the left
w: The left is blocked by the heart
Tubes are curved to the right
questions.e: Listening to both sides checks for it.

questions.q: ‘Auto-PEEP’ in asthma on a ventilator happens because?
questions.a: There’s not enough time to breathe out fully
questions.e: Air trapping can drop blood pressure. Disconnect and let them breathe out.

questions.q: Which electrolyte is given urgently for torsades de pointes?
questions.e: Even if the magnesium level is normal.

questions.q: Neuromuscular blockers stop movement but do not?
questions.e: Sedation must always come first: awareness is horrific.

questions.q: Sugammadex reverses which muscle relaxant by wrapping it up?
questions.e: It’s a ring-shaped sugar molecule.

questions.q: Succinylcholine can dangerously raise which blood level in burns or crush patients?
questions.e: From extra receptors spread across damaged muscle.

questions.q: Why might an ICU patient on long-term sedation get ‘ICU-acquired weakness’?
questions.a: Nerve and muscle damage from critical illness and immobility
questions.e: Early mobilisation helps prevent it.

theme: Hug it out: touch and oxytocin

questions.q: National Hugging Day: which hormone rises with hugs and touch?
questions.e: Sometimes called the bonding hormone.

questions.q: ‘Kangaroo care’ for newborns means?
questions.a: Skin-to-skin contact on a parent’s chest
w: Carrying in a pouch-like sling only
questions.e: It helps regulate temperature, breathing and feeding.

questions.q: Kangaroo care was pioneered in 1978 in?
questions.e: Bogotá, when incubators were scarce.

questions.q: Which touch receptors respond to slow, gentle stroking?
questions.e: They prefer touch at skin temperature.

questions.q: Oxytocin is released from which gland?
questions.e: It’s made in the hypothalamus.

questions.q: Oxytocin is also used in hospitals to?
questions.e: And to reduce bleeding after birth.

questions.q: Babies deprived of touch in old orphanages showed slowed growth. This is called?
questions.e: Growth often catches up with care.

questions.q: Which part of the skin has the highest density of touch receptors?
questions.e: The two-point test shows the difference.

questions.q: Hugs that last at least about how long are often quoted as most calming?
questions.e: Evidence is thin, but it’s a nice excuse.

questions.q: Weighted blankets mimic which kind of touch?
questions.e: Evidence for anxiety and sleep is mixed.

questions.q: Francis Bacon, born on this date, reportedly died after stuffing a chicken with?
questions.e: Testing whether cold preserves meat. He caught a chill, probably pneumonia.

questions.q: Moderate hypothermia starts below which core temperature?
questions.e: Mild is 32 to 35°C.

questions.q: ‘Nobody is dead until warm and dead’ refers to?
questions.e: Cold protects the brain. People have survived hours of CPR.

questions.q: ‘Paradoxical undressing’ in hypothermia happens because?
questions.a: Constricted blood vessels suddenly dilate, causing a feeling of heat
questions.e: Rescuers find people partly undressed in the snow.

questions.q: Frostbitten tissue should be rewarmed?
questions.a: In warm water, once there’s no risk of refreezing
questions.e: Refreezing does more damage.

questions.q: Brown fat generates heat using which protein?
questions.e: Babies have lots, around the shoulders and neck.

questions.q: Which part of the brain switches on shivering?
questions.e: It works like the body’s thermostat.

questions.q: Therapeutic hypothermia has been used to protect the brain after?
questions.a: Cardiac arrest and in newborns with oxygen starvation
questions.e: Benefit in adults is now debated; in newborns it’s standard.

questions.q: Cold urticaria causes?
questions.e: Jumping into cold water can be dangerous for these people.

questions.q: Chilblains (pernio) are?
questions.a: Itchy, red-purple swellings after cold exposure
questions.e: Rewarming too fast makes them worse.

questions.q: Elizabeth Blackwell became the first woman to earn a US medical degree on this date in?
questions.e: Her classmates voted to admit her, thinking it was a joke.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to qualify as a doctor in Britain, by passing the Apothecaries’ exam?
questions.e: The Society then changed its rules to stop other women doing the same.

questions.q: James Barry, a 19th-century British army surgeon, was found after death to be?
questions.e: Barry performed one of the first successful caesareans in Africa.

questions.q: Who was Australia’s first registered female doctor?
questions.e: She founded the Queen Victoria Hospital in Melbourne.

questions.q: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in physics and?
questions.e: She remains the only person to win in two sciences.

questions.q: Virginia Apgar’s score for newborns checks five things, including?
questions.e: Scored at 1 and 5 minutes.

questions.q: Gertrude Elion won a Nobel Prize for developing drugs including?
questions.e: She never finished a PhD.

questions.q: Which Australian nurse developed a controversial polio treatment using hot packs and movement?
questions.e: Her methods influenced modern physiotherapy.

questions.q: Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51 helped reveal the structure of?
questions.e: She died at 37, before the 1962 Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Françoise Barré-Sinoussi shared a Nobel Prize for discovering?
questions.e: With Luc Montagnier, in 2008.

questions.q: Moebius Syndrome Awareness Day. Moebius syndrome mainly affects cranial nerves?
questions.e: People can’t smile or move their eyes sideways.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve has the longest course inside the skull?
questions.e: Why it’s often affected by raised pressure.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is the only one to leave the back of the brainstem?
questions.e: It’s also the thinnest.

questions.q: Bell’s palsy affects which nerve?
questions.e: The forehead is weak too.

questions.q: Which nerve carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue?
questions.e: It passes through the middle ear.

questions.q: Trigeminal neuralgia causes?
questions.e: Carbamazepine is first-line.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve drives saliva from the parotid gland?
questions.e: Its fibres hitch a ride with a branch of the trigeminal to get there.

questions.q: A ‘down and out’ eye with a droopy lid and big pupil suggests a problem with?
questions.e: A painful one can mean an aneurysm.

questions.q: Shrugging the shoulders tests cranial nerve?
questions.e: It supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid.

questions.q: When the hypoglossal nerve is damaged, the tongue points?
questions.e: The healthy side pushes it over.

questions.q: Haggis, eaten on Burns Night, traditionally contains a sheep’s heart, liver and?
questions.e: Lungs are banned in haggis sold in the US.

questions.q: Haggis is traditionally cooked inside a sheep’s?
questions.e: Most now use synthetic casings.

questions.q: Which organ cleans your blood and makes bile?
questions.e: The largest internal organ.

questions.q: How many chambers does a human heart have?
questions.e: Two atria and two ventricles.

questions.q: Sweetbreads are usually the thymus or?
questions.e: Despite the name, they’re not sweet or bread.

questions.q: Tripe is the lining of a cow’s?
questions.e: Cows have four stomach compartments.

questions.q: Liver is very high in which vitamin, enough to be risky in pregnancy?
questions.e: Pregnant women are advised to limit it.

questions.q: Which organ, eaten as a delicacy, is the body’s main filter of urine?
questions.e: Steak and kidney pie, anyone?

questions.q: Robert Burns died aged 37, possibly of?
questions.e: His doctors also prescribed sea bathing.

questions.q: The lungs float in water because they’re full of?
questions.e: The French call them ‘mou’, meaning soft.

questions.q: Kawasaki Disease Awareness Day. Kawasaki disease mainly affects?
questions.e: Fever for five days or more is the key feature.

questions.q: Kawasaki disease can damage which blood vessels?
questions.e: Early treatment with immunoglobulin protects them.

questions.q: A child’s normal heart rate is?
questions.e: A newborn’s can be 120 to 160.

questions.q: A ‘hole in the heart’ between the lower chambers is a?
questions.e: Small ones often close on their own.

questions.q: Many children have harmless heart sounds called?
questions.e: They often come and go with fever or exercise.

questions.q: Which bacterial throat infection can lead to rheumatic heart disease if untreated?
questions.e: Rheumatic heart disease is still common in some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

questions.q: A blue baby may have a heart problem letting?
questions.e: Tetralogy of Fallot is a classic cause.

questions.q: Which test uses sound waves to see inside a child’s heart?
questions.e: Painless, often with a cartoon on the screen.

questions.q: Kawasaki disease is named after a doctor from?
questions.e: Tomisaku Kawasaki described it in 1967.

questions.q: Kawasaki disease often causes red eyes, a rash and?
questions.a: Red, cracked lips and a ‘strawberry tongue’
questions.e: Hands and feet swell, then peel.

questions.q: Mozart was born on this date. One theory blames his death on?
questions.a: Kidney failure after a strep infection
questions.e: Hundreds of theories exist; poisoning by Salieri is a myth.

questions.q: Why can a central line placed in the neck cause a pneumothorax?
questions.a: The lung’s top sits just behind the vein
questions.e: Ultrasound guidance makes this rarer.

questions.q: ‘Refeeding syndrome’ is dangerous mainly because of a sudden drop in?
questions.e: Feeding drives phosphate into cells. Start slowly.

questions.q: In sepsis, lactate rises partly because adrenaline?
questions.e: High lactate isn’t always from lack of oxygen.

questions.q: Hyperbaric oxygen is used for carbon monoxide poisoning and?
questions.e: Also some stubborn wounds.

questions.q: Why do burns patients need huge amounts of fluid early?
questions.a: Leaky capillaries lose fluid into tissues
questions.e: The Parkland formula estimates how much.

questions.q: ‘Permissive hypercapnia’ on a ventilator means?
questions.a: Allowing CO2 to rise to protect the lungs
questions.e: Small breaths avoid overstretching damaged lungs.

questions.q: Prone positioning (lying patients on their tummy) helps ARDS because?
questions.a: More lung gets air and blood together
questions.e: A 2013 trial showed lower deaths.

questions.q: Why might a patient with a very high sodium level need it lowered slowly?
questions.e: The brain adapts to the high level; rapid change draws water in.

questions.q: Correcting low sodium too fast risks?
questions.e: Damage to the brainstem: ‘locked-in’ in severe cases.

questions.q: Data Privacy Day. Which ancient oath includes keeping patients’ secrets?
questions.e: ‘Whatever I see or hear… I will not divulge.’

questions.q: In Australia, the national online health summary is called?
questions.e: People can set access controls or opt out.

questions.q: A doctor may break confidentiality when?
questions.a: There’s a serious risk of harm to someone
questions.e: And when the law requires, such as some notifiable diseases.

questions.q: Which diseases must doctors report to public health, even without consent?
questions.a: Notifiable diseases like measles and tuberculosis
questions.e: So outbreaks can be traced.

questions.q: At what age can a young person in Australia usually have their own Medicare card?
questions.e: Many get confidential care from teen years.

questions.q: A ‘mature minor’ can consent to treatment if they?
questions.a: Understand the treatment and its risks
questions.e: Sometimes called Gillick competence.

questions.q: Leaving patient notes on a public train is a breach of?
questions.e: Health data breaches must be reported in Australia.

questions.q: De-identified data means?
questions.a: Names and details removed so people can’t be identified
questions.e: Combined datasets can sometimes re-identify people.

questions.q: Which Australian law sets the main rules for health information held by private practices?
questions.e: Its Australian Privacy Principles cover collecting, using and sharing health data.

questions.q: In Australia, patients generally have the right to?
questions.e: There can be rare exceptions.

questions.q: National Puzzle Day. A woman with fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation most likely has?
questions.e: TSH is high.

questions.q: Fever, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash in a teenager means?
questions.e: Give antibiotics immediately.

questions.q: Sudden worst-ever headache, ‘like a thunderclap’, suggests?
questions.e: Needs urgent CT.

questions.q: A young man with back stiffness worse in the morning, better with exercise, has?
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain pattern.

questions.q: Red, painful big toe joint overnight after a big night out suggests?
questions.e: Uric acid crystals.

questions.q: Pain starting near the belly button then moving to the right lower abdomen suggests?
questions.e: The classic migration.

questions.q: A smoker with clubbing, weight loss and coughing blood needs checking for?
questions.e: Chest imaging is needed.

questions.q: Excessive thirst, weeing a lot and weight loss in a child suggests?
questions.e: Check a finger-prick sugar the same day.

questions.q: Painless jaundice with weight loss in an older adult raises concern for?
questions.e: Courvoisier’s sign: a palpable gallbladder.

questions.q: Tearing chest pain going to the back, with unequal arm blood pressures, suggests?
questions.e: An emergency.

questions.q: World NTD Day. About how many people are affected by neglected tropical diseases?
questions.e: Mostly the world’s poorest communities.

questions.q: River blindness (onchocerciasis) is spread by?
questions.e: Ivermectin, donated since 1987, has transformed control.

questions.q: Which NTD is spread by freshwater snails?
questions.e: Larvae burrow through skin in contaminated water.

questions.q: Trachoma, the leading infectious cause of blindness, is still found in?
questions.a: Some remote Aboriginal communities in Australia
questions.e: Australia is working to eliminate it.

questions.q: The ‘SAFE’ strategy for trachoma includes surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness and?
questions.e: Clean water and toilets.

questions.q: Lymphatic filariasis causes?
questions.e: Spread by mosquitoes.

questions.q: Which NTD was the 2015 Nobel Prize partly awarded for treating, with ivermectin?
questions.e: William Campbell and Satoshi Ōmura.

questions.q: Scabies was added to the WHO NTD list in?
questions.e: Common in remote Australian communities, where it can lead to kidney and heart disease.

questions.q: Snakebite envenoming was added as an NTD because it kills about?
questions.e: Antivenom access is the big problem.

questions.q: Which NTD causes ‘dog-bite’ deaths almost entirely preventable by vaccinating dogs?
questions.e: Almost always fatal once symptoms start.

questions.q: World Leprosy Day falls on the last Sunday of January. Leprosy is caused by?
questions.e: Gerhard Hansen identified it in 1873.

questions.q: Which animal can naturally carry leprosy in the Americas?
questions.e: Its cool body temperature suits the bacteria.

questions.q: Leprosy prefers cooler parts of the body, so it affects?
questions.a: Skin, nerves near the surface, nose and eyes
questions.e: Hence loss of eyebrows and a collapsed nose.

questions.q: Is leprosy highly contagious?
questions.a: No: most people are naturally immune
questions.e: Spread is mainly by droplets after long close contact.

questions.q: Multidrug therapy for leprosy includes rifampicin, dapsone and?
questions.e: Free from WHO since 1995.

questions.q: Clofazimine can turn skin?
questions.e: It fades after stopping.

questions.q: Why do people with leprosy lose fingers and toes?
questions.a: Numbness leads to unnoticed injuries and infection
questions.e: The disease itself doesn’t make digits fall off.

questions.q: Which famous Hawaiian settlement isolated people with leprosy?
questions.e: Father Damien worked there and died of leprosy.

questions.q: Leprosy’s Hansen’s disease name was promoted partly to reduce?
questions.e: ‘Leper’ is a stigmatising word to avoid.

questions.q: A leprosy reaction where nerves suddenly become painful and swollen is treated with?
questions.e: To prevent permanent nerve damage.

questions.q: Today’s date, written 11/23, gives the start of the Fibonacci sequence. Which number comes next after 5, 8, 13?
questions.e: Add the last two. That’s all of it, and medieval Italian rabbits never looked back.

questions.q: The ratio of neighbouring Fibonacci numbers closes in on the golden ratio, which is about?
questions.e: Beware anyone who says your navel proves it. The body is less tidy than the internet.

questions.q: Body mass index is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by?
questions.e: A population tool from Adolphe Quetelet in the 1830s, who was an astronomer and statistician, not a doctor.

questions.q: On a fictional chart, a 20 kg child is due paracetamol at 15 mg/kg. That dose is?
questions.e: 20 times 15. Yes, it’s that simple. And yes, people still check it twice, as they should.

questions.q: Adrenaline labelled 1:1000 contains how much per millilitre?
questions.e: One gram in 1000 mL, so 1 mg/mL. Generations of students have been saved by this sentence.

questions.q: A child on the 75th percentile for height is?
questions.a: Taller than about 75% of children the same age and sex
w: Likely to reach 75% of adult height soon
questions.e: Percentiles compare, they don’t grade. Please don’t tell parents their child is ‘only’ 40%.

questions.q: Normal saline, at 0.9%, contains how much sodium chloride per litre?
questions.e: That 0.9% means 0.9 g per 100 mL. Multiply by ten and feel clever.

questions.q: Smoking 20 cigarettes a day for 10 years comes to how many pack-years?
questions.e: One pack a day for one year is one pack-year. Twice the packs, twice the pack-years.

questions.q: In the adult ‘rule of nines’ for burns, one whole arm counts as?
questions.e: Each leg gets 18%. Handy to know, and it adds up to 100 with the groin’s lonely 1%.

questions.q: Virginia Apgar’s newborn score, taken at 1 and 5 minutes, has a maximum of?
questions.e: Five signs, up to 2 points each. An anaesthetist’s neat bit of arithmetic that has saved many babies.
